sentences.text: Stratesaurus was a small, early plesaur that reached a total length of two meters, with a skull measuring just eighteen centimeters.
Its snout was not constricted and held twenty-one tooth sockets in total, with five located in the premaxilla and sixteen in the maxilla.
The animal possessed unique, strongly developed projections on the front part of its neck vertebrae that pointed backward, alongside unusually short vertebral bodies in the shoulder region.
Fossils from its discovery site represent the earliest known occurrence of the plesiosaur group, making it one of the oldest known members.
The strongly developed backwards-pointing projections on the prezygapophyses in the front part of the neck are a unique feature not seen in other similar animals.
Benson, Evans, and Druckenmiller first described and named the genus in 2012, combining the historical name for Street from the Domesday Book with the Greek word for lizard.
The genus contains only one known species, Stratesaurus taylori, named to honor paleontologist Michael A. Taylor for his work preparing the holotype specimen.
The holotype specimen OUMNH J.10337 consists of a nearly complete crushed skull and a partial postcranial skeleton with vertebrae, a hindlimb, and an ilium, all collected at Street, Somerset.
Phylogenetic analysis places Stratesaurus as the most basal member of the Rhomaleosauridae family, which is classified within the order Plesiosauria, suborder Pliosauroidea.

The fossil record for Stratesaurus spans from 201.4 to 199.5 million years ago during the Hettangian stage, with the animal living approximately 199.6 to 198 million years ago shortly after the Triassic-Jurassic boundary.
